extracted.intended_audience: literary readers, critics, and writers (early 19th-century poetry and prose)
extracted.subtask_description: Epistolary literary criticism: norms and evaluative remarks on poetry, novels, translation, and reviewers' practice, as expressed in Charles Lamb's letters. Offers principles about tone, form, simplicity, reader-author relationship, and emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid_direct_didacticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructions conveyed in a poem should not be too direct or lecture-like; 'An intelligent reader finds a sort of insult in being told, "I will teach you how to think upon this subject."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: passages that 'put a sign-post up to show where you are to feel' (examples: Sterne and many modern novelists). Prefer works that allow ideas to insinuate themselves rather than overtly instructing the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: No_sign-posts_telling_readers_where_to_feel
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should not continually assume readers to be stupid by using explicit prompts such as 'Let not my reader suppose,' 'Imagine, if you can,' etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This habit breaks the implicit compact between author and reader and cheapens the reader's experience; avoid second-person signposting and overt stage directions about emotional response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor_the_implied_compact_with_readers
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an unwritten compact: 'I will tell you a story, and I suppose you will understand it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust readers' intelligence; present the narrative or poetic material without over-explanation so that understanding arises naturally from the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles_should_not_undercut_a_tale's_truth
rubrics_metrics.description: A title that signals unreality or self-consciously frames a tale (e.g., calling the 'Ancient Mariner' a 'Poet's Reverie') can 'subvers[e] of all credit' the tale should force upon us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose titles that preserve the tale's required credibility; avoid labels that pre-empt or distance the reader from the story's intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid_excessive_character_backstory_when_universal_effect_needed
rubrics_metrics.description: In works aiming for dreamlike or overwhelming supernatural experience, supplying the character with detailed profession/background can undermine the intended loss of individuality: 'the "Ancient Marinere" undergoes such trials as overwhelm and bury all individuality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the effect depends on universality or a dream-state, resist anchoring the protagonist with too much particularizing detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity_must_not_mask_poverty
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity of expression can be admirable, but 'you sometimes doubt if simplicity be not a cover for poverty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for genuine simplicity that arises from craft, not from an absence of richness or thought; beware of artful-seeming plainness that conceals thinness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional_impact_is_essential
rubrics_metrics.description: A volume lacking pieces that 'make you laugh or cry' is faulted; strong emotional effect (to move the reader) is a major merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value poems and stories that elicit clear emotional responses rather than cold technical cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness_can_be_a_strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Short pieces can exemplify the best work: 'The best piece in it I will send you, being short.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brevity that concentrates effect is praiseworthy; avoid gratuitous length that dilutes impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid_animate_scenery_and_continuous_echoes
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective descriptive writing can make mountains and scenery 'absolutely seem alive' and convey continuous echoes that animate the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use description that gives landscape active presence and that participates in the reader's feeling, as in Lamb's praise of passages where 'the mountains and all the scenery absolutely seem alive.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtle_imaginative_empathy
rubrics_metrics.description: A desirable poetic effect is when 'the mind knowingly passes a fiction upon herself, first substituting her own feeling for the Beggar's, and in the same breath detecting the fallacy, will not part with the wish.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate subtle moments where the reader imaginatively adopts a subject's feeling while retaining an ironic self-awareness; this tension is a refined pleasure in poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union_of_tenderness_and_imagination_as_high_poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'union of tenderness and imagination' (as Wordsworth describes, and ascribed especially to Milton by him) is presented as the highest species of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for work combining heartfelt feeling with imaginative reach; this union is a benchmark for poetic greatness in the letter's commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author_reading_own_work_can_reduce_effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet reading his own verses to an audience may lessen their effect: 'A poet that chooses to read out his own verses has but a limited power over you... There is a bound where his authority ceases.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about public self-performance—reading one's own work can expose its artificialities and invite derisive reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation_or_adaptation_should_preserve_continuous_power_and_rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: A good translation/adaptation maintains 'the continuous power of interesting you all along' and a metrical pacing appropriate to the original (example: Chapman 'gallops off with you his own free pace'; fourteen-syllable metre 'capable of all sweetness and grandeur').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating, prioritize sustaining the original's momentum, tone, and rhythmic effect rather than slavish literalism; preserve the text's capacity to engage continuously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism_may_focus_on_parts_when_whole_is_elusive
rubrics_metrics.description: Lamb confesses he 'cannot follow [an author's] train... I can vehemently applaud, or perversely stickle, at parts; but I cannot grasp at a whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers who naturally respond to parts rather than whole should not be obliged to produce systematic, comprehensive accounts; attentive, discriminating reactions to passages are legitimate critical practice.
